card.hook: You'll be admiring this staircase from the floor, and honestly that's part of its charm. It's the first stop on our Santa Fe map, and it rewards a little patience.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're in a tight space, so the whole staircase fits in one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. If your phone does 2x or more, use it for details of the staircase.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line a vertical edge up with a grid line so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Go when it's quieter if you can, because a gap in the crowd makes the shot easier. Check the official site for current visiting times.
card.selfie_here: Inside, stand on the chapel floor at the foot of the Miraculous Staircase with the stairs behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the staircase over your shoulder. Outside, stand on the sidewalk or plaza in front of the entrance at 207 Old Santa Fe Trail with the Gothic front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The staircase is roped off and you can't climb it, so stay on the floor. Photography inside and outside is for personal use only, so be considerate of other visitors. Rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole staircase, then one close-up of a detail, and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: Loretto Chapel and its staircase is the first numbered spot on the Santa Fe map. The phone icon marks the subject itself. Entry and photography rules can change, so it's worth a quick look at the official site before you visit.
card.stand_here_before_2026_11_13: Stand at Loretto Chapel and its staircase, right on the phone icon. It sits at the subject itself, so there's no walk. Step back a pace or two if you can, face the staircase and keep your phone level.

card.hook: Some buildings need clever tricks. This one just sits there in soft earthy adobe, looking calm and uncluttered, and your phone does the rest.
card.stand_here: Stand about 40 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Face the front of the building so the entrance is in view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole facade. If the pavement is narrow and you can't step back, try 0.5x, but keep the building square to the screen so the walls don't lean. Save 2x or more for details like the doorway or the wall texture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's edges up with the vertical lines, then put the entrance on one of the thirds instead of dead centre.
card.best_time: Go early or late in the day, when the street is quieter and the light is soft. When you arrive, check which side of the street is in the sun so the facade isn't stuck in harsh shadow.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x so more of the building fits in. Step back a little and tilt the phone so the walls sit over your shoulder, with the doorway in view if you can.
card.rules_and_safety: Indoor photography is restricted at the museum, so plan on taking your pictures outside. Check the official site before you go for opening and entry details.
card.challenge: Take three shots: the whole facade, the doorway, and a close-up of the wall so good you can almost feel the texture.
card.good_to_know: The museum is at 217 Johnson Street in the centre of Santa Fe, in an adobe-style building. It's a short walk from the Santa Fe Plaza, so it fits easily into a stroll around the centre. If people walk through your frame, wait a moment and they usually pass.
card.stand_here_before_2026_11_13: Stand on the pavement in front of the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum on Johnson Street (217 Johnson St), at the spot marked by the phone icon on the map, or just across the street if you can. Face the front of the building so the entrance is in view.

card.hook: Here's a spicy opinion: one guide says the Plaza itself isn't especially photogenic, because on the ground it's crowded and busy. The better shot is from above, looking down on it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 50 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. You'll be on the east side of the Plaza, looking west across the trees, the bandstand and the obelisk.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the cross, the city and the mountains in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the Plaza closer. Use 0.5x only if you want a big sky above the cross.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the top line, with the white cross low or off to one side.
card.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, which guides recommend for this hilltop. The walk up is paved and gently climbing, so leave yourself a little time and bring water.
card.selfie_here: Down on the Plaza, pose beside the obelisk in the middle with the square behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a bit lower and wider so the scene fits over your shoulder. Or stand under the covered portal of the Palace of the Governors with the Palace facade behind you. The shade there gives soft light for portraits.
card.rules_and_safety: If Native American artists selling under the Palace portal end up in your shot, ask their permission first. Check the official site before you go for any charges, local restrictions or events.
card.challenge: Take two photos that make a pair: the big view of the Plaza from the hill, then a close-up of the adobe walls and people through the portal.
card.good_to_know: Santa Fe Plaza is the open square at the heart of the old town, framed by historic adobe buildings and the arcaded portal of the Palace of the Governors. Guides say it's busy at weekends and during the summer market season. If you want a street-level shot too, the portal makes a good frame, with people and adobe walls in front.

card.hook: Picture a street of low adobe-style galleries with the hills waiting at the far end, like the street was built for your phone. That's Canyon Road, and you get a foreground, a middle and a distance without trying.

card.zoom: Start at 1x for the opening view along the street. Try 0.5x if you want more sky and road, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the hills or a gate without walking up to it.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the adobe wall, then slide the brightness down to darker a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Aim for the last 90 minutes before sunset, when the low light warms the adobe walls. Some guides suggest coming in the morning for the shadows, then returning in late afternoon to catch the other side of the road.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at the low sign where Canyon Road meets Paseo de Peralta, at the western end, and keep the sign behind your shoulder. It's close to the Plaza and most hotels, so it's an easy place to start. For a second selfie, find the old gate on the southwest corner of Canyon and Delgado and put it behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stick to the public sidewalk. Photo rules vary by gallery, so ask before photographing artwork or courtyards inside galleries.
card.challenge: Get one shot with the road in the lower middle and the hills along the top, then wait for a single walker to stroll into the foreground.
card.good_to_know: Canyon Road is a street of galleries in Santa Fe, with low adobe-style buildings along both sides. Guides suggest starting at the western end and walking east, so the mountains stay in front of you. Parking is limited, so arriving on foot helps.

card.hook: One small earthy tower, a stone wall and a huge slab of sky: San Miguel Chapel is almost unfairly easy to photograph. Don't just shoot the building, because the street is part of the picture too.
card.stand_here: Stand about 40 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The chapel's front will be right across the street, with the Pink Adobe restaurant behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the whole chapel front and a bit of street fit in. Go to 0.5x only if you need more street, and keep the chapel away from the edges so the lines don't stretch. If your phone has 2x, use it for the tower and the stone wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with one of the vertical lines so the walls stay upright.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters adobe walls. Go outside Mass times so you're not photographing during a service.
card.selfie_here: Go to the chapel entrance on Old Santa Fe Trail and stand in front of the bell tower over the door. Use the front camera (0.5x if yours has it) and hold it a little low so the tower rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the street, in front of the Pink Adobe at 406 Old Santa Fe Trail, while you stand by the chapel so the whole building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't photograph during services, as the chapel is consecrated. Stay on the public sidewalk and keep out of the Pink Adobe's entrance, because it's private. The chapel's own website says photos and videos are allowed, but asks you to be discreet and respectful. Keep an eye on passing people and traffic while you frame your shot.
card.challenge: Line the tower up with a gridline, then use a Live Photo to catch the moment a passer-by walks through your frame and picks the cleanest shot.
card.good_to_know: San Miguel Chapel is a small adobe church with a single tower and a stone wall around it. It sits on Old Santa Fe Trail, which also went by the older name College Street. It's consecrated and holds sacraments during Mass, so check current opening hours before you go.

card.hook: A giant metal wolf guards the front door, and honestly, that's your cue that you're in the right place. Your whole photo plan can start right there on the pavement.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It marks the venue itself, so there's no long walk or hunt for an angle.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the whole front. If you can't step back far enough, tap 0.5x to squeeze it all in. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out little details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest colour on screen, then drag the slider down to make it a touch darker so the colours stay rich instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Daylight is the easiest for clear, true colours outside. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone on something steady if you can find it.

card.good_to_know: Entry is likely to need a ticket, so check the official site before you go. Rules on photography, bags and entry can differ inside. The outside is usually the simplest place to take pictures freely.

card.hook: Picture a row of bright, cheerful sculptures marching you up to a museum door. That's the walk in to the Museum of International Folk Art, and it's better than most postcards.
card.stand_here: Stand about 420 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. You'll be looking south-west across to the museums on the hill.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a sculpture with the building behind it. Go to 0.5x if you want the whole facade and the sculptures in one shot. Zoom 2x is handy for picking out details on the building without walking anywhere.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep your phone level so the walls stay straight, then tap the sculpture and slide brighter/darker down a touch if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day is best. The softer light flatters bright colours and keeps harsh shadows off the facade.
card.selfie_here: Stand just in front of the tall entry portal at Milner Plaza (the Meem Entrance), so the museum's name carved above the doors is in the frame. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the portal and its painted quote over the silver doors fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the upper Milner Plaza, a few steps from the entrance and facing the museum front, to take your photo while you stand in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: The outdoor grounds are free to walk around, but the galleries are ticketed. Interior photos are generally fine without flash, though special exhibitions can have their own rules. Drones are generally not permitted on Museum Hill, so check before flying.
card.challenge: Find the one sculpture that sits between you and the door, give it one side of your frame, and see if you can keep the building's walls dead straight on the other.
card.good_to_know: The museum is at 706 Camino Lejo on Museum Hill. If you have time, take one frame in each spot: the garden gives you colour and detail, and Milner Plaza gives you the whole building framed by native grasses, Native American sculptures and the hills behind.

card.hook: Here's a trick that makes a plain hotel photo look like a postcard: stack it in three layers. Green benches at the bottom, portal columns in the middle, La Fonda behind.
card.stand_here: Stand about 45 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. La Fonda's adobe front will be right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole facade across the plaza. If the benches, portal and hotel won't all fit, tap 0.5x. Try 2x for a closer shot of the building's details without walking over.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone level so the building's vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Go at first light. The shadows fall across the portal columns and the crowds haven't arrived yet. Later the square gets busy, so wait for gaps or let people in on purpose to show scale.
card.selfie_here: Try the sidewalk on the Plaza side of La Fonda, in front of its Plaza frontage, where the hotel opens right onto the square. Use the front camera with the hotel behind you, and see if you can fit the fountains and the Obelisk in too. It's worth checking the view on your screen before you commit.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Plaza's southeast corner, facing La Fonda so the whole building is in frame, while you pose in front of the hotel.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza is public, but the hotel's interior spaces are private and commercial photography may need permission, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the benches, the columns and the hotel are all clearly visible, then see if a friend can spot all three layers.
card.good_to_know: La Fonda on the Plaza is the hotel beside Santa Fe Plaza, the city's central square. The portal is the covered walkway in front. Guides also point to the obelisk and fountains as part of the scene, so decide where you want them in your frame. The hotel is east of the phone icon, about 1 minute on foot, if you want a closer look at the entrance.

card.hook: Locals call it the Roundhouse, and one look at that big curved wall shows you why. Your photo is basically a portrait of a circle.
card.stand_here: Stand about 130 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Face the building head-on so the curve of the wall sweeps across your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole curved facade in. If you're close and it won't fit, drop to 0.5x, then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to tighten up on the carved State Seal over the doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and hold the phone level so the horizontal lines stay straight and the curve looks smooth.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to the facade. For the seal close-up, any clear daytime hour works.
card.selfie_here: Head inside to the middle of the rotunda floor and stand on the turquoise and brass State Seal mosaic. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little low, and let the stained-glass skylight and the ring of galleries rise up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally permitted inside the Capitol for personal use. Interior access is generally limited to weekdays, while the exterior and grounds can be visited on weekends, so check the official site for building hours and any legislative-session restrictions before you go.
card.challenge: Take a wide shot of the whole curve, then a close-up of the seal. Now sidestep a few paces and see if you can catch the facade looking totally different.
card.good_to_know: The Capitol's Territorial-style facade is round, which is where the Roundhouse nickname comes from. Each of the four entrance wings has a carved State Seal above the doorway. The grounds are planted with high-desert plants, sequoias and sculptures by Allan Houser, so step back for a shot with some greenery and art around the building.

card.hook: Most streets won't let you step back far enough to see a whole building. Santa Fe Plaza does, so you get the long, low, earthy Palace of the Governors in one go, with its wooden porch stretched along the front.
card.stand_here: Stand about 60 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. The long adobe front and its portal will be in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole Palace front with the obelisk in view. If you walk up close to the portal, switch to 0.5x to get the whole porch in one frame. Zoom 2x or more (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the carved beams and the artisans' displays, so you can keep a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the portal roofline along the upper or lower line, and keep the phone level so the long building doesn't slope.
card.best_time: Go early, at first light before the shops open. The plaza is calmest then, so the view of the building is clear and uncluttered. Later in the day, take your time and shoot between passers-by.
card.selfie_here: Pose by the obelisk in Santa Fe Plaza with the Palace's facade behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and wide (0.5x if your phone has it), and let the long adobe front fill the background over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: If any of the Native American artists selling under the portal end up in your shot, ask permission first. The plaza is open to everyone, but the Palace itself may have visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole portal in one frame with the obelisk off to one side and no strangers in it. Bonus points for patience.
card.good_to_know: The Palace of the Governors is the long, low adobe building on the north side of Santa Fe Plaza, at Palace Avenue. Native American artisans regularly set out their wares under its wooden portal, though stall positions change from day to day. Guides describe the plaza as the city's most photographed public space.

card.hook: The Oldest House is the opposite of a grand view: a low, earth-coloured adobe with a plain front and one small plaque doing all the bragging. That modesty is exactly why it makes such a nice, human-sized photo.
card.stand_here: Stand about 25 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Stand on the street facing the front wall, so the adobe, the plaque and the doorway are all in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and keep the whole front wall in the frame. If the street is too narrow to fit it all, try 0.5x. Then use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the plaque.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the adobe wall, then slide the brightness down a little if the bright sky is washing the walls out, because mud-coloured walls look richer slightly darker.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on adobe. Have a look at the street on the day you go, since it can vary.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and stand close so the adobe wall sits over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher and keep it level so the wall doesn't lean.
card.ask_someone: Ask your photographer to stand on the opposite side of East De Vargas Street, with the house's front wall and door in frame, while you stand in front of the house. Have them check the frame on the spot, since there's no exact standing point to copy.
card.rules_and_safety: The house is a museum, so opening arrangements may vary. Check the official site before you go, as this shot is taken from the public street.
card.challenge: Get the plaque and the doorway in one frame, then wait for a passer-by to wander through, because a little street life makes the small house look wonderfully tiny.
card.good_to_know: The plaque states the house's claim to age, but that claim is disputed, so treat it as part of the story rather than settled fact. The San Miguel Chapel is close by and can sit in the same scene. The street runs just east of Old Santa Fe Trail, so you can use it as a leading line.

card.hook: Picture two streets meeting at a corner, with a soft adobe-coloured building sitting right where they join. Guides often call it one of Santa Fe's most photographed buildings, and this corner gives you the classic postcard angle.
card.stand_here: Stand about 45 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. You'll see the Pueblo Revival front and both street sides meet at the corner.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole corner. If the pavement is narrow and you can't fit both street sides in, tap 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x for the wooden beams (vigas) and balconies.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the corner of the building up with one of the vertical lines, so the walls stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on adobe walls. Go when the pavement is quieter and you'll get a clear view of the corner.
card.selfie_here: The one selfie spot we have is inside, in the courtyard you reach first after entering the museum at 107 W Palace Ave. Stand with the frescoed walls and plants behind you, use the front camera, and hold it a little low so the paintings sit over your shoulder. Heads up: this gives you a leafy, painted backdrop, not the outside facade.
card.rules_and_safety: The courtyard is paid-entry, so check the official site before you go. Casual personal photography is allowed in exhibition areas, but flash attachments are not, so check the museum's current visitor policy before you rely on that.
card.challenge: Can you get the building's corner sitting exactly on a gridline, with a row of vigas poking out like little wooden fingers?
card.good_to_know: The museum stands on the northwest corner of the Plaza, where Palace Avenue meets Lincoln Avenue. It's built in the Pueblo Revival style, with adobe-toned walls, vigas and wooden balconies. For a straight-on view of the facade, walk along West Palace Avenue. Lincoln Avenue shows a quieter side, but it's the least proven angle, so treat it as an extra to try.

card.hook: Step off the Rail Runner and you're already standing in the photo: old depot, shiny tracks and a mountain line behind them. Not a bad start to a walk.
card.stand_here: Stand about 30 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Stand in front of the Santa Fe Depot on the track side, facing the platforms.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the depot, the platforms and any trains. Go 0.5x to fit in more track and sky. For the water tower or the mountain line, try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tracks up with one, so they lead the eye to the depot and mountains, and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day usually gives the mountain silhouette the most shape. Check which way the light falls when you arrive. If the water tower is your main picture, pick a day that isn't Saturday, because market booths can block it.
card.selfie_here: Head to the paved plaza in front of the restored wooden water tower and stand with the SANTA FE RAILYARD lettering behind you. Use the front camera at arm's length, and a Rail Runner train may be stopped on the track behind the tower.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is generally allowed in Railyard Park & Plaza, but commercial photography or filming may need a permit. This is an active train area, so stay alert and follow any posted restrictions around the tracks.
card.challenge: Get the tracks, the depot and the mountains all in one shot, then wait for a train to roll in and try again.
card.good_to_know: The depot is where the Rail Runner arrives, so it's an easy start for a photo walk around the Railyard. The water tower and Railyard Plaza are elsewhere in the Railyard, so plan a short stroll. On Saturdays the Artisans and Farmers markets set up near the water tower, and the Santa Fe Artists Market runs Saturdays from March to December. Check what's on before you go.

card.hook: Picture a calm, honey-coloured church with two matching towers and a round window right in the middle. The Cathedral Basilica is so symmetrical it almost poses for you.
card.stand_here: Stand about 85 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here you get the whole facade head-on with both towers.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full front. Try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the rose window and tower tops. Save zoom 0.5x for when you walk over to Cathedral Place, where the building is too tall to fit otherwise.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, centre the doorway, and keep your phone level so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset is your moment. The sun hits the stone at an angle and the whole front glows.
card.selfie_here: Head to Cathedral Park (131 Cathedral Place) and stand on the grass near the sandstone entrance pillars. Use the front camera and tilt it up so the twin towers rise over your shoulder through the trees. If you visit when the trees are in bloom, Bishop's Garden on the cathedral grounds is another pretty backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across from the main facade on the Plaza side, so the whole front fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship, so dress and behave respectfully. Interior photography is generally not allowed, especially during services, so plan on exterior shots and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get both towers perfectly balanced left and right, then take one more shot with a different amount of sky.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral is a Romanesque-style church in downtown Santa Fe, built of warm, honey-coloured stone. At Cathedral Place, in front of the church, a bronze statue of St. Francis stands in the courtyard. Cathedral Park is a shaded, grassy spot with benches if you want a leafier shot.

card.hook: You'll spot the red bridge before you spot the sign. It glows against the soft greens and browns of the high desert, and the colour does most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand about 60 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Then step a few metres along the path until the whole bridge is in frame, facing it with the piñon-juniper slopes and distant mountains behind.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole bridge over the arroyo. Try 0.5x for more slopes and sky, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pull the mountains in closer behind the bridge.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red of the bridge, then slide the brightness down a little so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the crowds are thinner.
card.selfie_here: Pose on or against the red bridge (Kearny's Gap Bridge), with the Sun and Moon Mountains over your shoulder. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit lower so the bridge fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are welcome throughout the garden, but photos taken there can't be used commercially without the garden's written approval. Dogs aren't allowed, and the Art Trail has uneven ground and one step, so watch your footing while you look at the screen. Check the garden's official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one with the bridge dead centre, then one with it on a gridline and the hills and sky filling the rest. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The bridge spans the Arroyo de los Pinos and was moved to the garden from a former highway site, so it has some local history as well as a strong shape. If you want something softer afterwards, the Orchard Gardens have fruit trees, wildflowers and grasses for texture and seasonal colour. The native piñon-juniper woodland shows off the open high desert.

card.hook: A tall cross against open sky is about the easiest subject you'll get all day, so even a quick snap can look good. Take a minute over it and it'll look even better.
card.stand_here: Stand about 20 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the cross and its setting. Want lots of sky or landscape? Try 0.5x, but keep the cross away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. If you can't get close, 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) gives a tighter, simpler shot.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the cross up with a vertical grid line so it doesn't lean, then tap the cross and slide the picture a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset gives softer, warmer light and a more interesting sky. Midday sun can turn the sky pale and flatten the shot.
card.selfie_here: Head for the cobblestone platform around the cross at the top of the paved path (617 Paseo de Peralta), a spot people use for sunset photos of Santa Fe. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and see if you can fit the cross over your shoulder. Check on site which way works best.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the paved switchbacks as they climb toward the cross, or on the level a few stairs below it, and shoot up while you stand by the cross.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear comfortable shoes, as the trails can be steep and uneven in parts. Access can vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots: the cross on its own, then one with the town or landscape behind it. Bonus points if the cross stands perfectly straight on a grid line.
card.good_to_know: The cross is marked on our map in Santa Fe, and the cobblestone platform around it is at the top of the paved path. This page doesn't give dates or details about its history. For the story of the cross and the people it commemorates, read any information board on site or the official local tourism pages.

card.hook: Walk up Guadalupe Street and the church simply appears: a plain, earthy adobe front with a bell tower on top and no fuss at all. That calm simplicity is exactly why it looks so good on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand about 85 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the straight-on view of the whole front. If the pavement feels tight, drop to zoom 0.5x to fit it all in, and keep the tower upright. Then try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the bell tower and doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the bell tower up with an upright grid line so the walls stay straight, then tap the church wall and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the clouds keep their detail.
card.best_time: Visitors say storm clouds and sunset light gave dramatic pictures, so a changeable sky is worth waiting for. Take a few frames of each shot, because the light can change quickly. One visitor found the church closed by late afternoon, so check opening hours before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head into the forecourt and stand in front of the church with the façade behind you. Visitors say the courtyard is full of photo ops, and the big statue of Our Lady of Guadalupe is right there too. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit the church over your shoulder, and check what's behind you before you click.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the entry to the forecourt, on the street side, and shoot toward the statue and church front so the whole façade and bell tower fit in the frame, while you stand in the forecourt in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the church is reported as forbidden, so keep your picture-taking outside. Check opening hours before you go.
card.challenge: Collect the set of three: a straight-on shot from the street, one with the statue in front, and a close-up of the bell tower. Bonus points if the sky is doing something dramatic in at least one.
card.good_to_know: The Santuario de Guadalupe is an adobe church with a bell tower, on Guadalupe Street in Santa Fe. A large statue of Our Lady of Guadalupe stands in the forecourt. Visitors also mention the courtyard and gardens as pleasant places to take pictures.

card.hook: Step off East Palace Avenue and the street suddenly feels far away: brick underfoot, fruit trees overhead, and a fountain tucked into a two-level adobe courtyard. It's small, so you can get wide shots and tiny details without moving much.
card.stand_here: Stand about 20 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Face the porches so the trees, benches and both storeys fit in one view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole courtyard in. Then try 1x for a natural look, and zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the fountain, a bench under the trees or the porch beams.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of a wall, then slide it a little darker so the sunny patches don't wash out.
card.best_time: Afternoon is the time to aim for here. The courtyard can get busy with diners and shoppers, so be ready to wait a moment for people to walk out of your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the central courtyard by the fountain with the fountain and courtyard buildings behind you. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your arm out so the backdrop fits over your shoulder. card.rules_and_safety: The restaurant patio takes up much of the courtyard, so be polite about people's meals and shoot around the tables. Shop hours or photo restrictions may apply, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a shot where the fountain sits on a gridline, the porches fill the background and not one dinner plate sneaks in. Bonus points if you make it look like you had the courtyard to yourself.
card.good_to_know: Sena Plaza's main entrance is at 125 East Palace Avenue. It sits within a group of adobe buildings (the Sena, Prince and Trujillo buildings) that face the street. For a scene-setter, step back out to the pavement and photograph the long adobe frontage with its portal.

card.hook: Picture an earthy adobe wall, dark carved wooden gates and a little ditch running along in front, all on a quiet street. This is said to be the most photographed home on Santa Fe's Historic Eastside, and you'll see why.
card.stand_here: Stand about 100 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the house, the gates and the ditch in one shot. Then try zoom 2x to home in on the carved gate and the wall texture. If the street feels tight, zoom 0.5x helps, but keep the gridlines on so the wall stays straight.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the wall, then make the picture a touch darker so the adobe keeps its colour, and let the ditch run through the bottom of the frame to lead the eye to the gates.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters adobe and carved wood. The street tends to be calmer then too.
card.selfie_here: Head to the first diversion gate on Acequia Madre Street, just east of Camino Don Miguel, about 10 yards before the corner, next to the historic plaque. Use the front camera and zoom 0.5x so the gate, the stone-lined ditch and the plaque all squeeze in behind you. It's an older tip, so check the gate and plaque are still there.
card.ask_someone: For a different shot, ask someone to take your photo on the bridge over the Santa Fe River where Alameda ends and Camino Cabra begins, with the Acequia Madre head gate a few yards upriver on the south side.
card.rules_and_safety: The house is private property, so take your pictures from the public sidewalk and don't step into the courtyard. It's a residential street, so keep your voice down. Stay on the walkways and be mindful of private property along the ditch.
card.challenge: Make the ditch a leading line: can you get it pointing straight at the carved gate, with a bit of sidewalk in the foreground?
card.good_to_know: Acequia Madre is both a street and an old irrigation ditch, and the ditch is about seven miles long, so no single spot shows all of it. The house here is a 1930s adobe. For more of the ditch story, Monsignor Patrick Smith Park is where it runs in the open behind the houses facing Canyon Road, but water flow and access there may have changed.

card.hook: Walk up past the gallery crowds on Canyon Road and the noise drops away. Then a big, soft-edged adobe church appears, leaning back against its hillside like it's had a long day.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the street, the church and the hillside in one go. Tap 0.5x if the building won't quite fit, and keep your phone level so the walls don't curve. Switch to 2x for close-ups of the walls and doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines so the walls stand straight, then tap the adobe wall and drag the slider a touch darker if the sky is bright so the earthy colour stays rich.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when the softer light warms the adobe. The upper end of Canyon Road is also quieter then, so fewer people wander into your frame.
card.selfie_here: Head into the garden in front of the adobe façade, near the Upper Canyon Rd. entrance at Camino Cabra. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it on the front, and keep the big adobe wall behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the corner of Upper Canyon Rd. and Camino Cabra, shooting toward the church front, while you stand in the front garden so the whole adobe building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Plan on exterior shots only, because the building may be closed.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the corner, then one close-up of the walls and doorway, and see if you can keep both perfectly straight with the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Cristo Rey Church is a large adobe church at the upper end of Canyon Road, on the street that carries its name. This end of the road is quieter than the gallery stretch lower down. Street numbers can vary, so check the address on the day rather than relying on one.
